Laboratory studies then showed leukopenia (TLC 1400/μL; ANC 1050/μL). Chest radiograph revealed new left upper-zone infiltrates. [Clinical segment 1] A 35-year-old man presented for routine follow‐up 11 years after a left total hip arthroplasty with a ceramic‐on‐ceramic articulation. Hip aspiration yielded 10,750 white cells/μL; all cultures were negative. Serum cobalt and chromium levels were within normal limits. A metal artifact reduction sequence MRI revealed a left periprosthetic soft‐tissue mass measuring 9 × 8 × 10 cm, without bony involvement or bone‐marrow edema.

input_text: [Clinical segment 1] A 65-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of a slowly progressive orbital mass causing left exophthalmia, left hemifacial pain, and progressive visual impairment culminating in total vision loss. Her medical history included 8 years of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, stage IIB cervical adenocarcinoma treated 3 years earlier with concurrent radiotherapy and weekly cisplatin, and well-controlled hypertension, dyslipidemia, and hypothyroidism. On examination, she had left exophthalmia with vision impairment and complete restriction of ocular motility. Anterior rhinoscopy, oral cavity, and neck examinations were unremarkable; nasofibrolaryngoscopy revealed a discrete medial bulging of the left nasal fossa lateral wall and a leftward septal deviation. Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbital region showed a soft-tissue density lesion occupying the left maxillary sinus with extension into the orbit, ethmoidal and sphenoid sinuses, and bone discontinuity of the maxillary, septal, sphenoid, ethmoidal walls, and pterygopalatine fossa. MRI demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left maxillary sinus, nasal cavity, ethmoidal sinuses, and intraorbital region, with bone disruption of the lateral and inferior orbital walls, extension through the inferior orbital fissure, invasion of the left cavernous sinus, diffusion restriction around the ophthalmic nerve, and anterior displacement of the extraocular muscles and vessels; these findings were considered highly suggestive of malignant neoplasm. [Clinical segment 1] An 89-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) and hypertension presented with acute speech disturbance and right-sided weakness. On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative.

[Clinical segment 2] Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal.

[Clinical segment 3] Noncontrast head CT showed early ischemic changes in the left insula and frontal lobe. CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory.

[Clinical segment 4] Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein (10.74 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL) with normal renal, liver function, and electrolytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis (10 cells/µL) and elevated protein (55 mg/dL) with normal glucose. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.

A working diagnosis of probable RICH was made.

Gram, periodic acid–Schiff, and iron stains were negative. Punch biopsies of the chest and thigh were consistent with pityriasis rosea.
